pedagogy.summary: Children convert between units of time — hours to/from minutes, minutes to/from seconds, years to/from months, weeks to/from days — including mixed quantities (3 hours 25 minutes = 3x60 + 25 = 205 minutes). The method is MULTIPLICATIVE (x60, x7, x12), using known number facts, and must resist the base-10 pull that assumes 100 seconds in a minute. The documented errors are additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, base-10 assumptions, and irregular groupings (months vary in length; a month is not exactly 4 weeks).
bestPractices: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (x60, x7, x12), not repeated addition
Convert mixed quantities in two parts: whole units x rate, then add the remainder (3x60 + 25)
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute, not 100
Handle the reverse (150 s -> 2 min 30 s) by dividing and expressing the remainder
Flag irregular units — months vary; about 4 weeks in a month is approximate, not exact
keyRepresentations: The x60 / x7 / x12 rate as a known-fact chain (36 ÷ 6 = 6, so 360 s = 6 min)
A number track for counting leap years / weeks
A bar model splitting a mixed quantity into whole units + remainder
commonMisconceptions: Uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative for conversions
Assumes base-10 (100 seconds in a minute, 100 minutes in an hour)
Thinks every month is exactly 4 weeks / all months are the same length
Converts a mixed quantity by ignoring the remainder or the second unit

learn.summary: Children convert between units of time — hours↔minutes, minutes↔seconds, years↔months, weeks↔days — including mixed quantities (e.g. 3 hours 25 minutes = 3×60 + 25 = 205 minutes). The core idea is MULTIPLICATIVE conversion (×60, ×7, ×12) using known number facts, and resisting the base-10 pull that wrongly assumes 100 seconds in a minute or 100 minutes in an hour. Reverse conversions require dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s). Documented errors are additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, base-10 assumptions, mishandling the remainder/second unit in mixed quantities, and treating every month as exactly 4 weeks.

activities.title: Multiply-then-combine with a conversion machine
feedback: If a learner gives 180 minutes for 3 h 25 min, ask where the 25 minutes went; have them add the remainder back: 180 + 25 = 205. A bar model separating the whole units (3 × 60 = 180) from the remainder (25) can make the two-part split visible when the leftover is dropped.
If a learner reads 150 seconds as '1.5 minutes', group the seconds into sixties: two complete sixties and 30 left, so 2 minutes 30 seconds — 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30.
If a learner answers '2 minutes' for 150 seconds, point to the 30 seconds still unaccounted for and ask what happens to them.
If a learner uses ×100 for hours→minutes, contrast their answer with grouping into sixties so the 60-grouping is visibly correct.
activities.rationale: A visible multiply-then-add computation with a reverse divide-with-remainder makes the multiplicative structure and base-60 grouping concrete, directly confronting the additive and base-10 errors documented for this topic; the bar model scaffolds the whole-units-plus-remainder split.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 1-2) documents that when converting units of time children may rely on additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, may assume base-10 (100 seconds in a minute / 100 minutes in an hour), and may think there are always exactly 4 weeks in a month; the method uses multiplicative reasoning and known number facts (e.g. 360 s = 6 min via the 6 times-table).

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its non-standard groupings of 60, 12, 7, which underlies base-10 conversion errors and difficulty coordinating mixed units.
learnerActions: Take a mixed quantity such as 3 hours 25 minutes and convert it: multiply the whole units by the rate (3 × 60 = 180 minutes), then add the remaining 25 to get 205 minutes.
State out loud whether you counted up or multiplied, and why multiplying is faster.
Work a reverse conversion: take 150 seconds, group it into sixties — two full groups of 60 make 2 minutes, with 30 seconds left over, giving '2 minutes 30 seconds'.
Test the tempting '100 to a minute' idea against grouping real seconds into sixties, and describe what goes wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting units of time is multiply (by the fixed rate) then combine the remainder — not counting up — and for seconds, minutes and hours the grouping is 60, not 100.

activities.title: Known-facts conversion with a base-10 trap item
feedback: For '1.5 minutes', re-ground on 60: 1.5 of 60 would be 90 seconds, not 150; 150 seconds is 2 minutes 30 seconds.
For '2 minutes', ask about the leftover 30 seconds.
For 8 weeks 3 days, confirm 8 × 7 = 56 then add the 3 loose days for 59.
activities.rationale: Targeted items with carefully chosen wrong-answer options can help surface which error a learner is making (base-10 vs dropping the remainder vs additive). Such items check and may provoke reasoning; use them alongside worked construction, since choosing an answer does not by itself show the learner can carry out the method independently.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its non-standard groupings of 60, 12, 7, which underlies base-10 conversion errors and difficulty coordinating mixed units.
learnerActions: Fill in conversions such as '3 h 25 min = ___ min' and show the multiply-then-add working.
Match a seconds amount (e.g. 150 s) to its minutes-and-seconds form.
Choose the correct reading of 150 seconds and explain why '1.5 minutes' (base-10 thinking) and '2 minutes' (dropped remainder) are both wrong.
Convert 8 weeks 3 days to days using 8 × 7 = 56, then + 3 = 59 days.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure conversions rest on known multiplication facts and on keeping the remainder; the common wrong answers to the 150-seconds item — '1.5 minutes' and '2 minutes' — correspond to base-10 thinking and to dropping the remainder.

activities.title: Irregular units: months, weeks and the calendar
feedback: If a learner converts months to days as ×28 or calls a month exactly 4 weeks, use the calendar to show months of 28, 30 and 31 days and distinguish the approximate month fact from the exact week-to-day fact.
activities.rationale: Addressing month-length variability with a concrete calendar directly targets the documented 'every month is exactly 4 weeks' misconception while keeping exact rates distinct from approximate ones.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 1-2) documents that when converting units of time children may rely on additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, may assume base-10 (100 seconds in a minute / 100 minutes in an hour), and may think there are always exactly 4 weeks in a month; the method uses multiplicative reasoning and known number facts (e.g. 360 s = 6 min via the 6 times-table).

Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.
learnerActions: Use a real calendar to count the days in several different months, including February, and record what you find: months have 28, 29 (February in a leap year), 30 or 31 days.
State why 'about 4 weeks in a month' is an approximation, not an exact conversion.
Contrast the exact fact (1 week = 7 days) with the approximate month fact, and explain how you would convert months to days versus weeks to days.
activities.intendedInsight: Some time units convert by exact fixed rates (7 days per week, 60 seconds per minute, 12 months per year) while month LENGTHS are irregular, so 'a month ≈ 4 weeks' cannot be used as an exact conversion to days.

activities.title: Pose-and-solve conversion word problems
feedback: Ask the learner to justify their chosen rate; if they add rather than multiply, prompt them to build the ×rate from a known fact.
Probe the remainder: 'Did you keep the leftover part, and where did it go in your answer?'
activities.rationale: Spoken or written word problems let a learner verbalise the method, which may expose additive-vs-multiplicative reasoning. On its own a spoken dialogue does not record whether the learner multiplied or added, so pair it with written working.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.
learnerActions: Read or hear a word problem (e.g. 'A film lasts 150 seconds — how long is that in minutes and seconds?') and solve it, saying each step aloud.
Explain for each problem which rate you used (×60, ×7, ×12) and how you handled any remainder or second unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Conversions apply in context; choosing the right rate and correctly expressing mixed/remainder answers is part of solving the problem.

constraints: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (×60, ×7, ×12), not repeated addition; for mixed quantities convert whole units × rate, then add or keep the remainder.
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour, not 100; the 100-to-a-minute idea should be shown wrong against real grouping, not merely stated wrong.
Handle reverse conversions by dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s), not rounding or dropping the leftover.
Keep exact rates (1 week = 7 days, 1 year = 12 months) distinct from the approximate month-to-weeks relationship; month lengths vary from 28 to 31 days.

Choosing a correct option in a matching or selection item checks reasoning but does not by itself demonstrate independent construction of the method; include tasks where the learner carries out and shows the conversion.
A fixed conversion poster or table can display the rates but does not let the learner compute and see the remainder form; treat it as a reference scaffold rather than the main activity.
A bar model (whole units + remainder) and a number track for counting weeks/leap years are optional representations that can scaffold the split and the counting, not required mechanisms.
Illustrative interactions (feeding units into a ×rate step, grouping seconds into sixties, a toggle offering the base-10 reading) are ways to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic in the source was checked and is correct: 3 × 60 + 25 = 205 minutes; 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30 → 2 minutes 30 seconds; 8 × 7 + 3 = 59 days; 1.5 minutes = 90 seconds (so reading 150 s as '1.5 minutes' is genuinely wrong, as intended).

The source probe 'Is 90 minutes the same as 1.9 hours?' is a base-10 trap counterexample; the correct answer is that 90 minutes = 1.5 hours (since 60 minutes = 1 hour), not 1.9 hours. Retained only as a discussion prompt note, never as a learner answer option; any feedback must state 1.5 hours.

The original keyRepresentation 'number track for counting leap years / weeks' is retained as an optional scaffold in constraints and may be built into a dedicated activity where counting weeks or leap years is practised.

The source's assertions that '3D adds nothing' and that a static image or dialogue 'can't' teach the computation are catalog fit judgements, not established facts; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits. Comparative efficacy or necessity of any single format is not established by the sources provided.

The sourceClaims on Activities 2 and 4 support the conversion content, the 'express answers appropriately' convention, and the documented errors, but do not validate the efficacy of selection/distractor items or spoken word problems; efficacy wording is kept conditional.

probeDeeper: 'You changed 150 seconds — is that 1.5 minutes or 2 minutes 30 seconds? Why?' (base-60)
'How did you turn 3 hours into minutes — did you count or multiply?'
'Is every month exactly 4 weeks? How many days are in this month?' (irregular units)
'Is 90 minutes the same as 1.9 hours? What is it really?' (base-10 trap counterexample)
assess.correctAnswer: 3 x 60 = 180, + 25 = 205 minutes; 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30 -> 2 minutes 30 seconds; 8 x 7 = 56, + 3 = 59 days — using multiplicative reasoning and correctly combining the mixed parts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes base-10 grouping — 100 seconds in a minute or 100 minutes in an hour
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-ground on 60 by grouping actual seconds/minutes into sixties; contrast the base-10 answer with the real grouping so 60 sticks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts 150 s as '1.5 minutes' or '1 min 50 s'; converts hours using x100

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative for conversions
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model x rate with known facts (3 x 60) built from a conversion table; show that multiplication is repeated addition made efficient.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts 3 hours by slowly counting up in 60s, or adds where they should multiply, and struggles with larger conversions

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the mixed quantity — ignores the remainder or the second unit (3 h 25 min -> just 180; 150 s -> '2 minutes' dropping the 30)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two-part split — convert the whole units, then add or keep the remainder; use a bar model separating whole units from the remainder.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 180 minutes for 3 h 25 min, or '2 minutes' for 150 seconds

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks every month is exactly 4 weeks / all months are the same length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a calendar to show months vary (28-31 days) and that about 4 weeks is approximate; keep the exact week-to-day fact distinct from the month facts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts months to days as x28, or states a month is exactly 4 weeks

responseLevels.gap: Converts by adding or by base-10 (100 to a minute); drops remainders; treats all months as 4 weeks.
responseLevels.full: Converts all four unit pairs multiplicatively, handles mixed quantities (whole units + remainder) and reverse conversions (division with remainder) correctly, resists base-10, and treats irregular units (months) correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Converts simple whole-unit cases multiplicatively, but slips on the base-60 grouping in reverse conversions or drops the remainder in mixed quantities.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set conversion problems and WATCH the method: (1) 'Change 3 hours 25 minutes into minutes — show me how.' (2) 'A programme lasts 150 seconds — write that in minutes and seconds.' (3) 'How many days are in 8 weeks and 3 days?' Watch whether they multiply by the right rate (x60, x7) and handle the remainder, or add up, assume base-10 (100 to a minute), or drop the mixed part.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 150-seconds item is the discriminator: a base-10 child answers '1.5 minutes', a drop-the-remainder child answers '2 minutes', a child using the 60-grouping answers 2 minutes 30 seconds. The mixed 3 h 25 min item catches additive reasoning and dropping the remainder.
